interviewQuestions.question: How does Rabin-Karp's rolling hash let it search for a pattern faster than recomputing a hash at every position?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The idea is to treat every fixed-length window of the text as a number — a polynomial over the character codes in some base B, taken modulo a large prime — and compare those numbers instead of comparing characters directly.

The naive way to get each window's hash is to sum m terms from scratch, which is O(m) per window and O(n·m) overall — no better than brute force. The rolling hash avoids that: sliding the window one character right only changes two things — the character leaving on the left and the character entering on the right. So the new hash is `(old_hash - departing_char × B^(m-1)) × B + arriving_char`, all mod the prime. That's a fixed handful of arithmetic operations, regardless of how large the window is.

So the total cost is O(m) to build the very first window's hash, then O(1) per subsequent window, for O(n) across the whole scan — O(n + m) altogether, matching KMP's guarantee on average, though Rabin-Karp's worst case is technically O(n·m) if collisions are adversarially forced.

The part I'd always flag unprompted: hashes matching is only *probable* evidence of equal substrings, not proof — so every hash match still needs a direct character comparison before you report it as a real match.

**Testing:** whether you understand the rolling hash as an O(1) update, not just "Rabin-Karp uses hashing."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Why must you always verify a Rabin-Karp hash match with a direct string comparison?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because a hash is a many-to-one mapping — an unbounded number of distinct strings can, in principle, collapse to the same hash value under any fixed modulus. Equal strings are guaranteed to produce equal hashes, but the converse — equal hashes implying equal strings — only holds with high probability, not certainty.

Concretely: with a modulus around 10^9 and reasonably random text, the odds of a false collision on any single comparison are tiny, maybe one in a billion. But "tiny" isn't "zero," and if the input isn't random — an adversary who knows your modulus and base can construct two different strings that collide on purpose — skipping verification turns a probabilistic algorithm into a silently wrong one on exactly the inputs where correctness matters most.

The fix costs almost nothing: the direct comparison only runs when hashes already agree, which is rare, so it doesn't change the average-case time complexity at all. It's one line of code that's the entire difference between "probably correct" and "always correct," and it's the single most common thing left out of a rushed Rabin-Karp implementation under interview time pressure.

A production hardening on top of this: run two independent hashes with different (base, mod) pairs and require both to agree before verifying — that multiplies two already-small collision probabilities together, making a false match astronomically unlikely even against a targeted adversary.

**Testing:** whether you treat hash equality as evidence to verify, not as proof, which is the core correctness discipline of any hash-based algorithm.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Correctness

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose Rabin-Karp over KMP, given they have the same average-case complexity?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd reach for Rabin-Karp specifically when the problem generalizes beyond single-pattern, single-dimension search, because its hashing model extends there far more naturally than KMP's character-by-character bookkeeping.

The clearest case is **multi-pattern search**: hash every pattern into a set up front, then make one pass over the text rolling the window hash forward and checking set membership at each position — that answers "does any of 500 patterns match here" in one O(n) pass. KMP doesn't generalize this way without switching to a different structure entirely, like Aho-Corasick.

Another case is **2D pattern matching** — searching for a small image or grid pattern inside a larger one — where you can hash each row (or block) and roll those hashes the same way, something that doesn't have a clean KMP analogue.

Where I'd pick KMP instead: whenever the input might be adversarial and I need a hard guarantee with zero probabilistic caveat — KMP's O(n+m) bound holds unconditionally, while Rabin-Karp's average-case bound assumes hash values behave close to randomly, which an adversary who knows your modulus can violate. So the honest framing is: KMP for a guarantee with no asterisk, Rabin-Karp when the *shape* of the problem (multiple patterns, multiple dimensions) plays to hashing's strengths.

**Testing:** whether you can articulate a real reason to prefer one over the other, rather than treating them as interchangeable because both are "O(n+m)."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: Your Rabin-Karp-based duplicate-detection service in production is returning occasional false positives on user-submitted text. How would you debug and fix that?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
First question: is there a verification step at all? An implementation that reports a match the instant hashes agree, without a direct character comparison, will produce exactly this symptom — rare, seemingly random false positives — and it's a surprisingly common thing to have dropped somewhere between the original design and a later refactor. I'd check that path first before assuming anything about the hash function itself.

If verification is in place and false positives still happen, then the bug is upstream: the verification comparison itself might be operating on the wrong slice (an off-by-one in the window bounds), or the rolling update has an arithmetic bug — a missed modulus wrap after subtraction going negative is the classic one — that corrupts the hash so it no longer corresponds to the text it's supposed to represent, in which case the "verification" is comparing against the wrong window and passing incorrectly.

I'd isolate this by logging the (position, hash, actual substring) triple whenever a match is reported, then manually confirming the substring against the expected pattern for a sample of reported matches. If the substrings genuinely don't match despite a passing verification step, the window-index bookkeeping is off; if verification is simply absent, that's the fix.

Longer term, if user-submitted text is adversarial-adjacent (e.g., attackers probing for collisions to evade duplicate detection), I'd add a second independent hash and require both to agree — collapsing the collision probability further — rather than relying on a single modulus an attacker might eventually reverse-engineer.

**Testing:** whether you can localize a probabilistic-algorithm bug to "missing verification" versus "broken verification," which are different bugs with different fixes.
